title: Indiaspora Warns Targeting H-1B Holders Poses 'Very Serious' Risk to US Economy
excerpt: The diaspora organisation's October 30 statement flagged five proposed curbs — and urged US leaders to reject anti-Indian rhetoric ahead of the midterms.
body:
• Indiaspora, the non-partisan diaspora organisation, warned in an October 30 statement that targeting H-1B holders could have "very serious consequences" for communities across the United States.
  • The statement flagged five proposed measures: petition fees above $100,000, wage-weighted lottery selection, scrapping the 60-day grace period, freezing H-4 spousal work permits, and fees up to $70,000 on OPT and STEM extensions.
  • Not all of these are merely proposals: the $100,000 H-1B payment is already in force and has been extended to September 21, 2027, and a wage-weighted selection rule was finalised in December 2025 for the FY 2027 cap season.
  • Indian nationals received 71% of approved H-1B visas in FY24, so any tightening lands overwhelmingly on Indian professionals and their families.

Indiaspora, the non-partisan organisation of Indian diaspora leaders, has warned that political efforts to target H-1B visa holders risk serious economic harm to the United States — and urged leaders across the political spectrum to reject anti-Indian rhetoric as the midterm election season heats up. The statement, issued on October 30, was reported by The Hindu BusinessLine and VisaVerge.

"H-1B workers from India have helped make America the world's innovation leader, generating billions for the American economy. Driving them away could have very serious consequences for communities nationwide, from major cities to small towns."

— Sanjeev Joshipura, Executive Director, Indiaspora

Who is affected

The H-1B programme is the main work route into the US for Indian technology and healthcare professionals, and Indian nationals made up 71% of approved H-1B visas in FY24, according to figures compiled by VisaVerge. The people in the line of fire are not only new applicants: Indiaspora's statement named early-career graduates, laid-off workers who rely on the 60-day grace period to find a new sponsor, and H-4 spouses — most of them women — whose work permits are part of many families' household income. Indiaspora also stressed that foreign professionals fill gaps domestic hiring cannot immediately cover, pointing to rural physicians and teachers in under-resourced areas such as the Mississippi Delta.

What Indiaspora flagged

The statement listed five measures: petition fees exceeding $100,000 for high-tech and healthcare employers; replacing the randomised lottery with a wage-weighted mechanism that could disadvantage early-career graduates; scrapping the 60-day grace period for laid-off foreign workers; freezing H-4 spousal work permits (EADs); and imposing fees up to $70,000 on Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM extensions.

Proposed is not the same as in force

The measures Indiaspora cited do not all have the same legal status, and the distinction matters for anyone planning around them. As VisaVerge's breakdown sets out, the $100,000 payment for certain H-1B petitions — created by Presidential Proclamation 10973 in September 2025 — is already in force, applies to new petitions rather than renewals, and has been extended for another 12 months, to September 21, 2027. The wage-weighted selection rule is also no longer a proposal: the Department of Homeland Security finalised it on December 29, 2025, and it applied to the FY 2027 cap season. Other items on Indiaspora's list, including the H-4 EAD freeze and OPT fees, remain proposals circulating in Congress and the administration.

What to watch

Indiaspora warned that scapegoating foreign talent for short-term political gains could hurt the US economy and undermine the strategic partnership between the US and India. The immediate arena is the November 3 midterm elections, in which all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are contested, and immigration rhetoric is running high. For H-1B holders and applicants, the practical position is unchanged by the statement itself: the fees and selection rules already in force still apply, and the proposals Indiaspora opposes would each need their own rule or law before they bite.
